Antibiotics should be used in rhinosinusitis only when acute bacterial infection is diagnosed and documented, not routinely for all cases of rhinosinusitis [doc1].

**When to diagnose acute bacterial rhinosinusitis:**

Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis should be diagnosed in patients in whom symptoms persist without improvement for **>10 days** after the start of URTI symptoms, or where symptoms worsen within 10 days after an initial period of improvement (i.e., "double sickening") [doc1]. This time-based approach is necessary because no individual symptom reliably distinguishes bacterial from viral infection—fever, purulent discharge color, and nasal symptoms all occur in viral infection [doc1].

**Preferred initial approach:**

Symptom management only is the preferred initial strategy for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis [doc1]. Approximately 70% of acute rhinosinusitis cases resolve within 2 weeks without antibiotics [doc1]. The number needed to treat (NNT) is 19—meaning 19 patients must receive antibiotics for 1 to benefit—while only 8 patients need antibiotics for 1 to experience side effects [doc1].

**Two antibiotic-sparing strategies** may minimize unnecessary use even when bacterial involvement is suspected [doc1]:

- **Intranasal corticosteroid trial**: Patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms may experience modest relief with intranasal corticosteroid spray; a 72-hour trial may avoid antibiotics altogether [doc1].
- **Watchful waiting**: Deferring antibiotics for up to 7 days after diagnosis while providing symptom management is safe and effective in appropriately selected patients, with reassessment guaranteed if illness persists or worsens [doc1]. Some clinicians provide a rescue prescription with instructions to start antibiotics only if symptoms fail to improve within 7 days or worsen [doc1].

**When antibiotics are clearly indicated:**

Patients with red-flag symptoms suggesting complicated disease (altered mental status, periorbital edema, exophthalmos, ocular pain, severe headache, neck stiffness, systemic illness) require further evaluation and antimicrobial therapy [doc1]. Additionally, antibiotics do not prevent complications—the complication rate is similar with or without antibiotic treatment [doc1].

**Shared decision-making** is essential, weighing the self-limiting nature of illness, low complication risk, and harms of unnecessary antibiotics (resistance, costs, adverse effects, *C. difficile* infection) [doc1].
